findings.who: A retiree, or on a joint return the spouse, whose 2025 monthly benefit went entirely to Medicare Part B/D premiums, federal tax withholding, a levy or garnishment, or recovery of an earlier overpayment. No benefit money reached their bank account in 2025.
findings.why_no: "did you ... get social security benefits": they received no payment, so they read the deductions as never having been benefits they got. Help text that names only the form does not fix this if they have misplaced it or did not look at it.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31: "You should receive a Form SSA-1099 showing in box 3 the total social security benefits paid to you"; p. 32 worksheet line 1: "Enter the total amount from box 5 of all your Forms SSA-1099 and RRB-1099"
findings.fix: Add to help: "Answer yes even if your benefits were used to pay Medicare premiums, withheld for tax, or kept by SSA to recover an overpayment, so you received no money. Box 3 of Form SSA-1099 still counts these amounts."

findings.who: A filer or spouse who received Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) in 2025, possibly as a retroactive award, and does not think of disability payments as 'social security benefits'.
findings.why_no: "social security benefits" reads to many people as retirement benefits. SSDI is a disability payment, and the help never names disability or survivor benefits.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31: "disability payments (including Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) payments)" ... "You must report the remaining $12,000 on line 6a."
findings.fix: Reword: "... get social security benefits (retirement, survivor, or disability (SSDI), including a back-payment for earlier years) ...". Also note that SSI is not included.

findings.who: A filer awarded benefits late, who in 2025 received a lump-sum back payment covering 2023–2024 and no other benefits in 2025.
findings.why_no: "In 2025": they treat the lump sum as benefits for earlier years, not 2025 benefits.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31, Line 6c: "If any of your benefits are taxable for 2025 and they include a lump-sum benefit payment that was for an earlier year..."
findings.fix: Say "received in 2025, including any lump-sum payment for earlier years".

findings.who: A railroad retiree, or the spouse, who received Form RRB-1099 (tier 1 social security equivalent benefits) and cannot tell whether their railroad annuity is 'treated as social security'.
findings.why_no: "railroad retirement benefits treated as social security" is a legal classification. The filer thinks of the annuity as a pension and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31: "If you received railroad retirement benefits treated as social security, you should receive a Form RRB-1099."
findings.fix: Ask about the fact the filer can check: "Did you get a Form RRB-1099 (not only RRB-1099-R) from the Railroad Retirement Board?"

locators: p. 32, Social Security Benefits Worksheet, line 1; p. 31, Lines 6a and 6b
p. 32, Social Security Benefits Worksheet, line 1; p. 31, Lines 6a and 6b, "Box 4 will show the amount of any benefits you repaid in 2025"

findings.who: A retired railroad worker, or that worker's spouse on a joint return, receives tier 1 railroad retirement benefits on Form RRB-1099 and no Form SSA-1099. The 2025 payments include a retroactive amount for 2023 or 2024.
findings.why_no: The question says 'The Form SSA-1099 says so in its description of the amount in box 3.' The filer has no SSA-1099, may not think of tier 1 railroad benefits as social security, and answers no. The RRB-1099 shows prior-year amounts in its own boxes, which the question never mentions.
findings.line: ssb.lump_sum (missed refusal; the lump-sum election that could lower taxable benefits is silently forgone)
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31, Lines 6a and 6b: 'If you received railroad retirement benefits treated as social security, you should receive a Form RRB-1099.' Line 6c: 'If any of your benefits are taxable for 2025 and they include a lump-sum benefit payment that was for an earlier year, you may be able to reduce the taxable amount with the lump-sum election.'
findings.fix: Did the 2025 social security or tier 1 railroad retirement benefits paid to you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) include a payment for an earlier year? Form SSA-1099 shows this in the description of the box 3 amount. Form RRB-1099 shows it as amounts paid in 2025 for earlier years.

findings.who: An SSDI claimant was approved in 2025 with back pay to 2023. SSA paid part of the back pay directly to the claimant's attorney as fees and withheld part to offset SSI already received. The claimant got only a small check or none.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether benefits 'paid to you' included a payment for an earlier year. The filer reads 'paid to you' as money they actually received and answers no, even though the withheld and redirected amounts count as benefits paid to them.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31, Line 6c: 'they include a lump-sum benefit payment that was for an earlier year, you may be able to reduce the taxable amount with the lump-sum election.' Also p. 31: 'Form SSA-1099 showing in box 3 the total social security benefits paid to you.'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Count back pay for earlier years even if part of it went to an attorney or was withheld to repay SSI or an overpayment.'

findings.who: A disability award was decided and paid in 2025. It covers months in 2024 and 2025 and is paid as one retroactive lump sum.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks of the award as a 2025 payment because it was decided and paid in 2025. They do not read the help's pointer to the box 3 description and answer that nothing was 'for an earlier year.'
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 32, Social Security Benefits Worksheet TIP: 'If any of your benefits are taxable for 2025 and they include a lump-sum benefit payment that was for an earlier year, you may be able to reduce the taxable amount.'
findings.fix: Name the common case in the question: 'This includes back pay from a disability or retirement award that covers months before 2025.'

locators: p. 31, Line 6c; p. 32, Social Security Benefits Worksheet, TIP
